section.title: Job Replies to Zophar
section.sectionRationale: This long reply closes the first cycle of speeches. Job answers Zophar's claim to superior wisdom with biting sarcasm, then pivots to a sweeping vision of God's sovereignty over nations and kings, a fierce rebuke of his friends as worthless physicians, and finally a resolve to plead his case before God directly, whatever the cost. The unit ends with the book's first flicker of resurrection hope: if a man dies, will he live again?
section.thesis: Job matches his friends' claims to wisdom with his own, insists that God's sovereign power is plain even to animals and birds, resolves to argue his case before God though it may cost him his life, and, staring at the brevity and finality of human death, dares to ask whether a man could live again after dying.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: Job's sarcastic dismissal of the friends' claimed monopoly on wisdom; his sweeping description of God's sovereignty over nations, kings, and counselors; his rebuke of the friends as worthless physicians who would do better to stay silent; his resolve to defend his case before God though He slay him; his direct plea that God withdraw His hand and stop hiding His face; his meditation on the brevity of human life compared to a tree that can sprout again after being cut down; and his closing question, if a man dies, will he live again, followed by lament that hope, like eroding stone, wears away.

units.label: Wisdom will not die with you
units.note: ask the animals, and they will instruct you

verses.text: Then Job answered:
"Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die!

But I also have a mind; I am not inferior to you. 
Who does not know such things as these?

I am a laughingstock to my friends, though I called on God, and He answered. 
The righteous and upright man is a laughingstock.
The one at ease scorns misfortune as the fate of those whose feet are slipping.
The tents of robbers are safe, and those who provoke God are secure, those who carry their god in their hands.
But ask the animals, and they will instruct you; ask the birds of the air, and they will tell you.
Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you; let the fish of the sea inform you.
Which of all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?
The life of every living thing is in His hand, as well as the {{ruach|breath}} of all mankind.
Does not the ear test words as the tongue tastes its food?
Wisdom is found with the elderly, and understanding comes with long life.

units.label: Wisdom and strength belong to God
units.note: He makes nations great and destroys them

verses.text: "Wisdom and strength belong to God; counsel and understanding are His.
What He tears down cannot be rebuilt; the man He imprisons cannot be released.
If He holds back the waters, they dry up, and if He releases them, they overwhelm the land.
True wisdom and power belong to Him. The deceived and the deceiver are His.
He leads counselors away barefoot and makes fools of judges.
He loosens the bonds placed by kings and fastens a belt around their waists.
He leads priests away barefoot and overthrows the established.
He deprives the trusted of speech and takes away the discernment of elders.
He pours out contempt on nobles and disarms the mighty.
He reveals the deep things of darkness and brings deep shadows into light.
He makes nations great and destroys them; He enlarges nations, then disperses them.
He deprives the earth's leaders of reason and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland.
They grope in the darkness without light; He makes them stagger like drunkards.

units.label: Worthless physicians
units.note: if only you would remain silent

verses.text: "Indeed, my eyes have seen all this; my ears have heard and understood.
What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you.
Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and argue my case before God.
You, however, smear with lies; you are all worthless physicians.
If only you would remain silent; for that would be your wisdom!
Hear now my argument, and listen to the plea of my lips.
Will you speak wickedly on God's behalf or speak deceitfully for Him?
Would you show Him partiality or argue in His defense?
Would it be well when He examined you? Could you deceive Him like a man?
Surely He would rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality.
Would His majesty not terrify you? Would the dread of Him not fall upon you?
Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.

units.label: Though He slay me, I will hope in Him
units.note: I will still defend my ways to His face

verses.text: "Be silent, and I will speak. Then let come to me what may.
Why do I put myself at risk and take my life in my own hands?
Though He slay me, I will hope in Him. I will still defend my ways to His face.
Moreover, this will be my salvation, for no godless man can appear before Him.
Listen carefully to my words; let my declaration ring in your ears.
Behold, now that I have prepared my case, I know that I will be vindicated.
Can anyone indict me? If so, I will be silent and die.

units.label: Why do You hide Your face

verses.text: "Only grant these two things to me, so that I need not hide from You:
Withdraw Your hand from me, and do not let Your terror frighten me.
Then call me, and I will answer, or let me speak, and You can reply.
How many are my iniquities and sins? Reveal to me my transgression and sin.
Why do You {{sathar|hide}} Your face and consider me as Your enemy?
Would You frighten a windblown leaf? Would You chase after dry chaff?
For You record bitter accusations against me and bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth.
You put my feet in the stocks and stand watch over all my paths; You set a limit for the soles of my feet.
So man wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment.

units.label: Man is short of days and full of trouble
units.note: there is hope for a tree

verses.text: "Man, who is born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble.
Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure.
Do You open Your eyes to one like this? Will You bring him into judgment before You?
Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one!
Since his days are determined and the number of his months is with You, and since You have set limits that he cannot exceed,
look away from him and let him rest, so he can enjoy his day as a hired hand.

For there is hope for a tree: If it is cut down, it will {{tsemach|sprout}} again, 
and its tender shoots will not fail.
If its roots grow old in the ground and its stump dies in the soil,
at the scent of water it will bud and put forth twigs like a sapling.
But a man dies and is laid low; he breathes his last, and where is he?
As water disappears from the sea and a river becomes parched and dry,
so a man lies down and does not rise. Until the heavens are no more, he will not be awakened or roused from sleep.

units.label: If a man dies, will he live again?
units.note: so You destroy a man's hope

verses.text: "If only You would hide me in Sheol and conceal me until Your anger has passed! If only You would appoint a time for me and then remember me!

When a man dies, will he live again? All the days of my hard service I will wait, 
until my {{chaliphah|renewal}} comes.
You will call, and I will answer; You will desire the work of Your hands.
For then You would count my steps, but would not keep track of my sin.
My transgression would be sealed in a bag, and You would cover over my iniquity.
But as a mountain erodes and crumbles and a rock is dislodged from its place,

as water wears away the stones and torrents wash away the soil, 
so You destroy a man's hope.
You forever overpower him, and he passes on; You change his countenance and send him away.
If his sons receive honor, he does not know it; if they are brought low, he is unaware.
He feels only the pain of his own body and mourns only for himself."

ruach.gloss: Breath, wind, spirit, the animating life-force God gives to every living thing. Job argues that even the animals know the hand of the LORD holds the ruach of all mankind, a truth so basic it needs no elaborate philosophy, only observation of the created world.

sathar.gloss: To hide, conceal. Job's anguished question, why do You hide Your face, becomes one of the most repeated laments in the Psalms; here it names the specific pain of feeling treated as an enemy by a God who will not show Himself or explain.

tsemach.gloss: A sprout or shoot, new growth from what appeared finished. Job observes that even a felled tree can sprout again at the scent of water, a hope explicitly denied to human beings in this chapter, which sharpens rather than answers his coming question about life after death.

chaliphah.gloss: A renewal, relief, or change, from a root meaning to pass on or be replaced. Job's hope that his chaliphah will come, after his hard service is finished, is one of the boldest and most fragile hopes in the entire book, reaching toward the possibility of life after death without yet having any certainty of it.

basic.context: Job answers Zophar's claim to superior wisdom with sharp sarcasm, insisting he knows everything the friends know, and that even the animals and birds understand that the LORD's hand governs all things. He then paints a sweeping picture of God's total sovereignty over nations, kings, counselors, and priests, before turning to rebuke his friends bluntly as worthless physicians who would do better to stay silent. He resolves to argue his case before God directly, even at the risk of death, uttering one of the boldest statements of faith in the book, though He slay me, I will hope in Him. He then meditates on the brevity of human life, noting that even a felled tree can sprout again but a dead man does not rise, and dares to ask the question the whole book has been building toward: if a man dies, will he live again?
basic.hermeneutics: This speech shows Job's faith deepening even as his theology remains unresolved. His declaration of hope even if God slays him is not naive optimism but a bold trust that persists without any promise of rescue. His question about life after death is not answered here, and should not be forced into a fuller resurrection doctrine than the text itself claims; it is a genuine, aching question, a seed that Scripture's later revelation will bring to full flower.
basic.originalLanguages: Job argues that even creatures know the ruach, breath, of all mankind rests in God's hand. He asks why God will sathar, hide, His face and treat him as an enemy, a lament that becomes a fixture of the Psalms. He observes that a tree can tsemach, sprout, again after being cut down, but longs, without certainty, for his own chaliphah, renewal, after death, one of the most poignant unanswered hopes in the Old Testament.
basic.typology: Job's question, if a man dies, will he live again, plants a seed that will not fully bloom until the New Testament's clear revelation of bodily resurrection in Christ. His declaration, though He slay me, I will hope in Him, anticipates the kind of trust that holds even when God's actions look like abandonment, a trust perfected in Christ's own submission in Gethsemane.
basic.christ: Job's trembling question about life after death finds its full and certain answer in the resurrection of Jesus Christ, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, proof that the hope Job could barely dare to voice is in fact secured. Where Job could only wish for a time appointed and a remembering, the gospel announces the day fixed and the Redeemer who has already risen, guaranteeing that all united to Him will rise as well.
basic.god: God is described here in totalizing sovereign terms, tearing down what cannot be rebuilt, humbling kings and counselors, yet Job experiences that same sovereignty as terrifying rather than comforting, since it currently seems turned against him. The tension between God's greatness and God's apparent hostility remains unresolved, driving Job's daring resolve to plead his case directly rather than to give up.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 answers Job's question directly, Christ the firstfruits of the resurrection of the dead; Psalm 13:1 echoes Job's lament, how long will You hide Your face from me; Habakkuk 3:17-18 models a similarly bold trust, though the fig tree does not blossom, yet I will rejoice in the LORD.
basic.oneStory: Job's fragile, daring question, if a man dies, will he live again, is one of the great unresolved hopes of the Old Testament, and the whole of Scripture moves to answer it fully in the bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ. His declared trust, though He slay me, I will hope in Him, models the kind of faith that holds on even without an answer, until the answer finally comes.

context.literary:
Three chapters, one reply, and the longest single speech in the first round. It is the widest in range, since it swings from sarcasm to a hymn, from a hymn to a courtroom vow, from the vow to an elegy on mortality, and it ends with the most quiet lament in the first cycle. The movement follows a pattern that will define Job's speeches: he turns from the friends to God, and each time he turns he says something he could not have said in front of them.

Chapter 12 has two panels. Verses 2 to 12 are aimed at the friends, and end with a proverb about the elderly that Job quotes only to set aside. Verses 13 to 25 then shift into a catalogue of God's overturning acts, in which counsellors, judges, priests, elders, nobles and whole nations are stripped and led away. The list is built on a repeated pattern of a strong person losing a strength that belonged to their office: the counsellor his counsel, the judge his judgment, the priest his standing, the elder his speech. It is a hymn, but a grim one, and it reads like Psalm 107 turned toward the downfall of the great.

Chapter 13 is the trial. It begins with the same claim, What you know, I also know, verse 2, which closes the friends' argument and opens Job's, and it uses a run of legal terms: argument, plea, indict, vindicated. Verses 13 to 19 are the commitment and verses 20 to 28 are the two requests, then the accusation.

Chapter 14 is a different key. It has no addressed audience until verse 3, and then it is the quietest voice in the book so far. Its verses run in pairs, a statement about man and a statement about a tree, and the heart of it is the contrast between verses 7 to 9 and verses 10 to 12, where the tree that sprouts again is set against the man who does not. The final verses, 18 to 22, tell how mountains crumble and hope with them. The first cycle ends in a sigh, and the last word is about pain that is felt only by the one who suffers it.
context.historical:
The physicians of verse 4 are a real class of Job's world. Medicine in the ancient East was a mixture of herbs, bandaging and prayer, and Egyptian and Mesopotamian practice blended the medical and the religious. Jeremiah asks, Is there no balm in Gilead, no physician there, Jeremiah 8:22, and the Chronicler criticises King Asa, who in his illness sought the physicians and not the LORD, 2 Chronicles 16:12. To be called a worthless physician was to be told that one's remedy was useless, and that what one applied to a wound was a false cure.

The hired hand of 14:6 is the day labourer, who worked from sunrise until his wages were paid at sunset, as the law required, Deuteronomy 24:14-15. Job asks God to let him have the rest of a day labourer at evening, the small satisfaction of a finished shift. The image is domestic and modest, and it shows how little Job now asks.

The trees of verses 7 to 9 belong to the Mediterranean world where olive stumps, willows and similar trees send up fresh shoots after being cut. A farmer who saw a stump sprouting near a wadi would take it as the ordinary wonder of a tree that will not die. Against this, the ancient view of death was bleak. The dead went to Sheol, a land of silence where the praise of God ceased, Psalm 88:10-12, and few in Job's age looked for any return. The prayer of 14:13, to be hidden in Sheol until God's anger has passed, is therefore a startling thing, since it treats the place of the dead as a shelter with an end.

The nations of 12:23 are the great powers Job's readers knew, rising and falling in the unstable politics of the region. Job's list of kings, judges and priests being led away barefoot recalls the way conquered peoples were marched off in captivity, and gives the hymn a historical edge.
context.canonical:
The birds and animals of 12:7 to 9 who know that the hand of the LORD has done this belong to the same Bible that sends the sluggard to the ant, Proverbs 6:6, and that hears the heavens declare the glory of God, Psalm 19:1. Creation is a teacher in the Scriptures, and Job's use of it is a fair one. The difference is that he uses it to say what the friends had said with less understanding, that God's power is written into everything, and he draws from it the opposite conclusion, that this power cannot be said to favour the upright in every case. The life of every living creature is in His hand, verse 10, and Paul sounds the same note in Athens when he says that God gives everyone life and breath and everything else, Acts 17:25.

The long list of overturned rulers in 12:17 to 25 has an echo in Psalm 107:40, which uses almost the same words, that He pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland. It also foreshadows Daniel, who says that God changes the times and seasons, removes kings and establishes them, Daniel 2:21. Job's grim description of God's sovereignty over rulers is what the prophets will sing as comfort for a people under empires.

The great vow of 13:15 is one of the most quoted lines of Job. It is echoed in the psalms of the righteous who say, though the earth give way, we will not fear, Psalm 46:2, and in the prayer of the Servant, in Gethsemane, Not My will, but Yours be done, Luke 22:42.

And the question of 14:14, When a man dies, will he live again, reaches forward to the prophets who say that many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, Daniel 12:2, and to the first resurrection of the Lord, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The Old Testament plants the question, and the New Testament plants a cross and an empty tomb in its answer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet gives Job his most sustained speech to show that the sufferer's faith is neither a simple certainty nor a simple doubt. It is a struggle with two poles, and the struggle is where faith lives. On one side, Job trusts God enough to stand before Him, verse 13:15. On the other, he cannot see a way that God could be for him, 13:24 and 14:18 to 20. The author does not let either pole win in this chapter, and he does not want the reader to settle it too soon.

The author also wants the reader to see the limits of the friends' resource. The three men have used up tradition, vision and doctrine, and Job answers that he knows all that, and that God's power to overturn is exactly what worries him. The friends' wisdom does not get a hearing after chapter 12. Job turns to God, and the book from that point on is a book about a conversation between a man and God that the friends cannot join.

And the poet is interested in the question of death. Nothing in the first cycle has gone as far as the question in 14:14. The first hearers, who lived without a clear teaching on resurrection, would have felt its daring. A man is asking whether the story could go on, and he is putting the question to the One who alone could answer it. The author leaves it open on purpose, to be taken up in Job 19, and to be answered in the rest of the Bible.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage describes a sufferer talking, and we have to sort what is said. Job's statement in 13:15 is a model of trust and can be taken up as such: to keep faith in God, and to keep speaking to Him, when everything looks like abandonment. Job's insistence on speaking to God rather than about Him is a pattern the Psalms confirm, and the epistle of James commends his perseverance, James 5:11.

By contrast, several things in the passage are not to be copied. The claim that God treats a person as an enemy, 13:24, and that He destroys hope, 14:19, are the perceptions of a man in pain, and God will not affirm them in His answer. The description of death in 14:10 to 12 says that a man lies down and does not rise, which is a description of how death looks from inside the Old Testament, and not a doctrine that the New Testament leaves standing. We are not asked to believe that no one rises. We are shown a person who did not yet see it, and who asked.

And Job's rebuke of his friends is descriptive as well. His words about their lies are not a licence to answer all counsel with contempt, though God's own verdict at the end shows that the friends had earned a rebuke.

debates.question: Does Job say, Though He slay me, I will hope in Him, or, I have no hope (13:15)?

views.label: I will hope in Him
views.case: The BSB, the King James tradition and many commentators read the line as an act of trust that survives death. The next clause, I will still defend my ways to His face, and verse 16, this will be my salvation, make a positive reading natural. It fits Job's courage in the whole passage.

views.label: I have no other hope, or I have no hope
views.case: The BSB footnote gives Or I have no other hope. The Hebrew text has a reading tradition in which one small word can be understood as not or as to Him, so ancient and modern translators divide. On this reading Job is saying he is finished, but even so will argue his case.

debates.bearing: The context favours a defiant trust, since a man with no hope at all would not argue his case to God's face. Even on the other reading the outcome is the same, that Job will speak to God, and the line remains a picture of faith at its narrowest.

debates.question: How much does Job hope for life after death in 14:13 to 15?

views.label: A real, if fragile, hope of resurrection
views.case: Job wants God to hide him in Sheol, set a time and remember him, and he says he will wait for his renewal, You will call, and I will answer. This is the language of a man who imagines being called back, and many Christian readers hear it as an early glimpse of resurrection, joined to Job 19:25-27.

views.label: A wish he immediately abandons
views.case: Verses 18 to 22 close the chapter in despair, with hope destroyed and the dead unaware of their children. On this view verses 13 to 17 are a daydream, a what if, that Job knows will not come true, and the text should not be read as any doctrine of resurrection.

debates.bearing: The two are not exclusive. Job dreams of a resurrection and then denies himself the dream, and the shape of the chapter is the honest oscillation of a mind that has no revelation to lean on. The New Testament does not need to be found in the verse, but the verse shows why it was needed.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is the laughter. In 12:4 Job says he is a laughingstock to his friends, using the same Hebrew word, sechoq, that Bildad used when he promised that God would fill Job's mouth with laughter, Job 8:21. In eight chapters the word has moved from a promise to a taunt. The one who was promised laughter has become the object of it. The reader is meant to hear both uses together.

In 12:6 the strange phrase about those who carry their god in their hands has a footnote in the BSB, which offers an alternative, that God brings them into their power. Both readings speak of the wicked who are secure, and the difference is whether the secure man makes his own god of his strength or is given his prosperity by God. Either way, Job is asserting a fact the friends deny, that the wicked can sit at ease.

The list of gifts in 12:13, wisdom, strength, counsel and understanding, is a compact summary of what a king or a judge needs. The verses that follow say that God takes each of them away from the officeholders who possess them. In verse 24 the trackless wasteland is the word tohu, the same word as the formless void in Genesis 1:2. The image is of powerful men wandering in an uncreated waste, and it matches the way the psalmist put it, Psalm 107:40.

In 13:8 the friends are accused of showing partiality. The Hebrew idiom is to lift up the face, the same phrase as in Zophar's promise that Job would lift up his face without shame, Job 11:15. To lift someone's face is to favour them, and Job tells the friends that they are lifting God's face in the way a corrupt judge favours a powerful party. God does not need it, he says, and He will rebuke it.

The controversy in 13:15 lies in a single small word. The consonants can be read as not, so that the sentence says he will not hope, or as to Him, so that the sentence says he will wait for Him. The BSB takes the second and marks the first in a footnote. The choice is one of the most discussed in the book, and the safest attitude is to see that both readings have Job continuing to speak to God's face.

In 14:1 the man born of woman is full of trouble, and the word for trouble means agitation or turmoil, the shaking of a life. Verse 4, Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one, uses the language of ritual purity for the whole human condition, and Psalm 51:5 gives the same thought in confession.

The word for a tree that sprouts again in 14:7 is from a root meaning to renew or to change, and Job's own longing in verse 14 uses a noun of that same root, chaliphah. The tree renews and the man asks for his renewal. The wording ties the two halves of the chapter together and makes the point that what a tree does by nature, Job can ask only by grace. The tree's hope, tiqvah, is the same word by which Job, in verse 19, says that God destroys the hope of a man.

Finally, in 14:15 the desire God will feel for the work of His hands is a word for longing. It is a remarkable thing to say of God, that He will yearn for the creature He made, and it is the emotional counterpoint to the earlier, colder words about God hiding His face.

typology.type: The tree that sprouts again, Job 14:7-9
typology.fulfillment: Job's tree, cut down and yet able to bud at the scent of water, is a picture of renewal that the prophets turn into a promise about a person. Isaiah sees a shoot spring up from the stump of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1, and Jeremiah and Zechariah call the coming King the Branch, Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 6:12, and the Hebrew name Branch, tsemach, means a sprout, the very picture Job holds up in these verses. The fulfilment is the resurrection of Jesus, the shoot from a dead stump. The type falls short because Job's tree only returns to its old life, while Christ's rising opens a new one in which death has no place.

Job's vow to trust God even if God kills him anticipates the obedience of the Son in Gethsemane, Not My will, but Yours be done, Luke 22:42. The parallel deepens in Isaiah 53:10, where it was the LORD's will to crush the Servant, and He did so as a guilt offering. What Job feared as an unjust act of God, the Father does in love for the world, and the Son accepts. The type falls short because Job trusts in ignorance of the reason, whereas Christ goes to the cross knowing exactly why, and for whom.

typology.type: The clean from the unclean, Job 14:4
typology.fulfillment: Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one, Job says, and the Bible agrees for every human being. The New Testament announces the One who can. In the Gospels, Jesus touches a leper and makes him clean, Mark 1:40-42, and the writer of Hebrews says that the blood of Christ cleanses our consciences, Hebrews 9:14. Where uncleanness usually passes to whoever touches it, in Christ the flow is reversed. The type falls short because Job states the impossibility as a fact of human nature, while the gospel shows a way in which the impossible is done by God Himself, at cost.

typology.type: Sheol as a hiding place until anger passes, Job 14:13
typology.fulfillment: Job's wish to be hidden in Sheol until God's anger has passed, and then remembered at an appointed time, is fulfilled in a startling way in Christ's death and burial. He went into the grave under the Father's judgment on sin and was raised on the third day, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, at the appointed time. Peter says that it was not possible for death to keep its hold on Him, Acts 2:24. The type falls short because Job asks this for himself and by wish, but Christ does it as substitute, and through Him the same hope is offered to those who are His, John 5:28-29.

study.christ:
Job 12 to 14 bring the first cycle to a close on a note that Christ answers most directly. The question of 14:14, When a man dies, will he live again, is asked without any promise behind it. The gospel does not need a hint from Job to say yes, but it gives the question a face. Jesus says to Martha, I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies, John 11:25, and Paul writes that Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The word firstfruits matters. It says the harvest follows, and Job's wait for his renewal is included in it.

The second link is the tree. The stump that sprouts again is one of the Bible's strongest images for the Messiah, the shoot from the stump of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1, and the righteous Branch whom the LORD will raise up for David, Jeremiah 23:5. Job's observation that there is hope for a tree, which he could not extend to a man, is fulfilled in the one Branch whose rising extends to all who belong to Him.

The third is the vow of 13:15 and the two requests of 13:20 to 22. Job asks that God withdraw His hand and terror, and that God either call or let him speak. The Christ of Gethsemane and the cross says, in effect, both. He goes to God's face with an honest cry, Mark 15:34, and He submits, Luke 22:42. Hebrews says that in the days of His flesh He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and was heard, Hebrews 5:7. Job's struggle to keep faith while God seems to kill him is met and completed in the Son, who was in truth slain by the will of the Father, Isaiah 53:10, and who remained the Son.

The fourth is the claim in 13:18 that Job will be vindicated. The apostle uses that word of Christ, who was vindicated by the Spirit, 1 Timothy 3:16, and he says that Christ was raised for our justification, Romans 4:25. Job's confidence about his cause is answered in a greater vindication that he shares by faith.

All of this should be said with care. Job is not Christ, and the tree is not a coded prediction in the way a prophecy is. The book of Job creates a series of aches, for a mediator, for a Redeemer, for a resurrection. The New Testament does not treat them as riddles solved by clever exegesis, but as needs met by a person. When we read these three chapters, the right response is to see how exactly the shape of the gospel fits the shape of the hole Job describes.
study.god:
The passage puts two very different pictures of God side by side, and does not try to reconcile them at once. In chapter 12 God is the sovereign who rules everything. The life of every creature is in His hand and the breath of all mankind, verse 10. Wisdom and strength are His, He tears down what cannot be rebuilt, He holds back waters and releases them, He makes nations great and destroys them. Not a single ruler, priest or judge holds a position that He has not given and cannot take away. The teaching is reinforced elsewhere, for Daniel says that He removes kings and establishes them, Daniel 2:21, and Paul says that He gives everyone life and breath and everything else, Acts 17:25.

In chapter 13 the same God appears as the party of a lawsuit, hiding His face and treating a leaf as an enemy. That is Job's perception, and Scripture does not say it is true of God, but it does say that God allows it to be spoken. The Psalms give the same cry to the faithful: Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction, Psalm 44:24. God's silence is part of how believers meet Him, and the Bible is honest about that.

Then chapter 14 introduces a third picture, small and easily overlooked. In 14:15, Job imagines God calling and himself answering, and says that God will desire the work of His hands. It is an insight into God's heart that Job has not been given from anywhere, and it is right. The God who made human beings does not lose interest in what He has made. The reader will recognise this as the character of God in the prophets, where He says, How can I give you up, Ephraim, Hosea 11:8, and in the gospels, where He seeks the lost.

What holds these together? The book does not say yet, but it gives clues. God allows the sufferer to say anything, and does not silence him. He rebukes the friends who defend Him falsely, and approves Job's speaking to Him, Job 42:7. And when at last He answers, He does so as the same sovereign that Job described in chapter 12, but with a tenderness in the questions and the creatures He brings forward. The sovereignty and the longing are one God.

For worship, the passage teaches us to bring both truths to God without prettifying either. We can say that He rules everything, and we can say that we cannot see what He is doing, and He will hear both. A worship that has no room for chapter 13 will not survive a real loss, and one that has no room for chapter 12 will have no one to bring its grief to.

crossReferences.note: He pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland. This is almost the same line as Job 12:21 and 12:24. In the psalm it is one of the ways the LORD rescues the poor and humbles the proud. Job says the same about God's power, but with no deliverance in sight.

God changes the times and seasons, removes kings and establishes them. It gives the positive side of Job's catalogue of overturned rulers, in the mouth of a prophet who is living under empires. Sovereignty over kings is a comfort when you are the one under them.

Paul says that God gives everyone life and breath and everything else. It echoes Job 12:10, that the breath of all mankind is in His hand. Paul takes the same fact to Athens as a call to worship the God who cannot be served like an idol.

Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression? The prayer uses the same language as Job 13:24 and shows that the question is at home among the faithful. The psalm is spoken by a community that has kept the covenant and still suffers.

Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me, yet not My will, but Yours be done. Jesus' prayer joins a request and a surrender in one breath. It is the fulfilment of the spirit of Job 13:15, in which a sufferer refuses to leave God's presence even when God seems to be the cause.

Surely I was brought forth in iniquity. David confesses the same condition Job states in 14:4, that no one can bring clean out of unclean. In the psalm it leads to a prayer for cleansing, and this shows where Job's impossibility finds its way: not to despair, but to a request for what only God can do.

A shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse. The prophet takes the picture of a cut-down tree that buds again and makes it a promise about the royal line. Job's hope for a tree becomes, in Isaiah, the hope of a people, and finally of a Person.

The LORD will raise up for David a righteous Branch who will reign wisely. The Hebrew name Branch, tsemach, means a sprout, the picture Job holds up in 14:7 to 9. It shows how the prophets could turn a natural image into a title for the Messiah.

Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake. This is the Old Testament's clearest statement of bodily resurrection, and it answers the question of Job 14:14 in the plainest terms. Job asked it in the dark, and Daniel is given the answer in vision.

Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. Paul supplies what Job lacked, a risen man whose rising guarantees the rest. Job's if a man dies, will he live again receives the answer that he does, because Christ did.

Jesus says, I am the resurrection and the life. He says it at the tomb of Lazarus, a place where every human hope had ended, and He says it about Himself. It takes Job's wait for his renewal and gives it a person and a voice that calls.

study.oneStory:
Job's meditation on the short life of man is an echo of Genesis 3. The man made from the dust, who was given the breath of life, Genesis 2:7, is now a flower that withers and a shadow that does not last, Job 14:2. The sentence of Genesis 3:19, to dust you shall return, sits behind every line of chapter 14. The rest of the Old Testament joins the lament: the grass that flourishes in the morning and fades by evening, Psalm 90:5-6, and the flower of the field that the wind passes over, Isaiah 40:6-8. Job's chapter is the Bible's shortest account of what the fall did to a creature made to live.

Job's questions also mark the place where the Old Testament story reaches its edge. The problem is not just that people die but that no one on earth can bring anyone back. Job asks it of God, and the prophets begin to answer, Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Between Job and Daniel lies a slow unfolding of hope, from a wish for a hiding place in Sheol to a promise that many who sleep in the dust will awake.

The resurrection of Jesus is the moment that story turns. In Him, the first man of the new creation is raised, and Paul can say that as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive, 1 Corinthians 15:22. The tree that Job envied has become a promise. And the creation that was subjected to futility is waiting in hope for freedom from its bondage to decay, Romans 8:19-21. What Job saw in a stump by the water, Paul sees across the whole cosmos.

The end of the story is the tree of life, the one that stands on either side of the river in the city of God, with leaves for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. Adam was barred from the tree of life, Genesis 3:24, and here it is given back. In that city the one who has been through the trouble of chapter 14 finds that God has called and that he has answered, and that the work of God's hands has been desired to the end. The hiding of God's face becomes the seeing of it, and the limits on man's days are lifted.

sermon.title: If a Man Dies, Shall He Live Again?
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly on Job 13:20-24 and 14:7-17, the exact heart of this passage, drawing out the comfort of God's presence, the challenge of His glory, and the joy of the resurrection as the resources Job reaches for even without full answers.

quiz.q: How does Job answer Zophar's implicit claim to superior wisdom in 12:1-3?

options.text: With sarcasm, insisting he is not inferior to them and that even the animals and birds understand the truths they claim as special insight.
options.note: Job's opening mocks the friends' assumption that wisdom belongs uniquely to them, verses 2-3 and 7-9.

options.text: By declaring plainly that he has a mind of his own and knows exactly what they know.
options.note: A true part of Job's response, though less complete than his sharper sarcastic appeal to the animals and birds.

options.text: By apologizing for his earlier complaints.
options.note: Job does not retract his earlier laments; he intensifies his case and his resolve to bring it before God.

options.text: By admitting his friends know far more than he does.
options.note: Job explicitly claims equality with them, not inferiority.

quiz.q: What bold statement of trust does Job make in 13:15?

options.text: Though He slay me, I will hope in Him, and I will still defend my ways to His face.
options.note: This is one of the most quoted verses in the book, expressing trust that persists even under threat of death.

options.text: He resolves to keep speaking and let come to him what may, since no godless man can appear before God anyway.
options.note: A true and closely related resolve from the same passage, though less precise than the exact wording of trusting God even if slain.

options.text: I am certain God will never harm me further.
options.note: Job's statement assumes the real possibility of being slain; it is trust despite danger, not a claim of guaranteed safety.

options.text: If He slays me, I will finally curse Him as my wife suggested.
options.note: This is the opposite of Job's actual declaration; he affirms continued hope rather than cursing God.

quiz.q: What contrast does Job draw between a tree and a man in 14:7-12?

options.text: A felled tree can sprout again at the scent of water, but a man who dies does not rise in the same way.
options.note: This contrast sharpens rather than resolves Job's coming question about whether a man could live again after death.

options.text: A tree has real hope of new growth even after being cut down, while a man who dies simply lies down and does not rise.
options.note: A close restatement of the same contrast, though slightly less precise than the exact detail about the tree budding at the scent of water.

options.text: Neither trees nor men have any hope of renewal.
options.note: The tree explicitly does have hope of sprouting again; the man's case is presented as the harder, contrasting one.

options.text: Both trees and men are guaranteed to be restored after death.
options.note: The passage explicitly denies this for man, which is exactly what makes Job's question in verse 14 so pointed.

quiz.q: What question does Job ask in 14:14, and how does Scripture ultimately answer it?

options.text: If a man dies, will he live again; the New Testament answers this fully in the bodily resurrection of Christ, the firstfruits of all who will rise.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 presents Christ's resurrection as the guarantee of the very hope Job could only tentatively voice.

options.text: Whether there is any renewal after his hard service on earth is finished, a hope Scripture later confirms in Christ's resurrection.
options.note: Correctly points toward Job's chaliphah, renewal, and its answer in Christ, though less exact than the precise question of verse 14 itself.

options.text: A question Scripture never actually answers.
options.note: The New Testament answers this question with unambiguous clarity in the doctrine of bodily resurrection secured by Christ.

options.text: Whether Job's children will be restored to him in this life.
options.note: The question in 14:14 concerns life after death in general, not the specific restoration of his own children.

quiz.q: What rebuke does Job give his friends in 13:4-5?

options.text: That they smear with lies and are worthless physicians, and that remaining silent would actually be their wisdom.
options.note: This is one of Job's sharpest direct rebukes of his friends' counsel in the entire book.

options.text: That their maxims are proverbs of ashes and their defenses are defenses of clay.
options.note: A true and vivid rebuke from the same speech, though less direct than Job's explicit charge that they smear with lies.

options.text: That they have not suffered enough to understand him.
options.note: Job's specific complaint here is about the falseness and uselessness of their arguments, not primarily about their lack of personal suffering.

options.text: That they should speak even more than they already have.
options.note: Job says the opposite, that silence would have been wiser than what they have said.

questions: Job insists that even animals and birds know basic truths about God's sovereignty that his friends claim as special wisdom. Where have you seen simple, obvious truths get lost under layers of clever argument, in yourself or others?
Job declares, though He slay me, I will hope in Him. What would it look like for you to keep trusting God even in a situation where the outcome looks like it could go very badly?
Job asks God directly to reveal his sin rather than assume it, and to stop hiding His face. Where do you need to bring a direct, honest question to God rather than settling for silence or assumption?

Job's question, if a man dies, will he live again, is answered decisively in Christ's resurrection. How does the certainty of resurrection change the way you face your own mortality or grieve the death of someone you love?

Job calls his friends worthless physicians who would have done better to stay silent. When you comfort someone in pain, how do you discern when to speak and when silence would truly be the wiser gift?

translationNotes.note: Breath renders ruach, the same word used of the Spirit of God elsewhere in Scripture; here it names the life-force God gives and sustains in every living creature.

This verse is textually debated in the Hebrew manuscript tradition, with some ancient witnesses reading 'I have no hope' instead of 'I will hope in Him'; the BSB, like most modern translations, follows the reading of confident trust, which fits the flow of Job's continued resolve to argue his case before God in the following verses.

Renewal renders chaliphah, from a root meaning to pass on or be replaced; the word carries a sense of relief or exchange, Job hoping for a change from his current hard service to something new after death, without yet full certainty of what that change would be.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Job 12:1-14:22. no other substantive changes were made to the verse text.
